items.title: Strait of Hormuz area (Bandar Abbas vicinity), Iran: Evidence of Iran's ad hoc transit arrangements surfaced: Iraq reportedly facilitated a Greek-owned VLCC on May 10, and at least 16 vessels used Iran's route on May 19-20, including Chinese, South Korean, Turkish, and Indian ships. Some European countries have proposed a post-war security force for the strait, but a NATO official told Bloomberg that at least some European states are concerned about the economic consequences of the closure.

items.rawSummary: Iran is cementing its contested administrative and fee-based control over Strait of Hormuz shipping, while the U.S. blockade has turned away 94 vessels and global economic fallout intensifies with fertilizer prices surging and stranded ships mounting.
items.analysis: Iran’s effort to entrench control over the strait is gaining traction, with evidence of ad hoc transit agreements—such as Iraq facilitating a Greek-owned VLCC on May 10—and at least 16 vessels using the Iranian route on May 19-20, according to commercially available shipping data. Transit volumes have increased moderately, though LNG shipments remain suspended, and ADNOC’s CEO called the closure the most severe supply disruption on record. The UAE’s presidential advisor rejected Iran’s jurisdictional claims over Emirati waters, while India disclosed that 14 of its vessels are stranded and said it would wait for safer conditions. The U.S. blockade has redirected 94 ships and disabled four as of May 21, up from 90 the previous day, according to U.S. Central Command, and U.S. forces recently seized an Iranian-linked tanker near the Strait of Malacca. Meanwhile, some European governments have discussed a post-war security deployment, but Iran would likely resist such a force, and a NATO official told Bloomberg that at least some European states are concerned about the economic consequences of the closure, particularly as world fertilizer prices surge 44%, threatening a new wave of food inflation.

items.title: Iranian regime governmental centers (unspecified locations), Iran: Pakistani Field Marshal Munir is set to visit Tehran today, but only if indicators suggest real progress can be made on the current proposal.
items.description: Pakistani Field Marshal Munir is set to visit Tehran today, but only if indicators suggest real progress can be made on the current proposal.
items.rawSummary: Iran’s nuclear negotiations remain deadlocked as conflicting claims over a reported Supreme Leader uranium directive coincide with a hardline bounty bill and reported IRGC consolidation of negotiation influence.
items.analysis: Nuclear diplomacy remains deadlocked over a disputed directive from Supreme Leader Khamenei. Reuters, citing senior Iranian officials, reported that the leader had ordered Iran’s near-weapons-grade uranium not to be transferred abroad, a move contradicting a U.S. demand and allegedly driven by concerns about vulnerability to further Israeli and American strikes. The White House and a senior Iranian official both denied the report. Meanwhile, Majlis hardliners introduced a bill offering a €50 million bounty for the assassination of President Trump and Prime Minister Netanyahu, and an assessment cited by the Associated Press indicates that IRGC commander Vahidi has consolidated influence over Iran’s negotiating position and military response, with a greater willingness than pragmatist officials to accept the risk of renewed conflict. Pakistan’s army chief conditioned his visit to Tehran on signs of real progress in the talks. Oil prices briefly climbed above $100 a barrel before falling back.

items.analysis: Iran has exploited the ceasefire to repair dozens of ballistic missile sites, relocate launchers, and adapt air defense tactics, while drone production resumed within weeks and rebuilding is outpacing U.S. intelligence projections, according to The New York Times and CNN. Tamir Hayman of the Institute for National Security Studies noted that Iran repaired the Fordow facility, accelerated work at the buried Pickaxe Mountain site, and accumulated an estimated 2,500 ballistic missiles, as the elevation of Mojtaba Khamenei with IRGC backing signals a more radical nuclear posture. Reuters reported that Supreme Leader Khamenei has ordered highly enriched uranium to remain inside the country, reversing earlier export signals, while the Congressional Research Service tallied 42 U.S. aircraft lost or damaged and $2.6 billion in equipment costs. Economic pressure from the naval blockade has intensified, with Iran reusing aging tankers for oil storage and officials voicing public frustration, alongside an 80-day internet blackout and recent executions. The combination of rapid military recovery and Tehran's refusal to compromise on its nuclear materials is narrowing the diplomatic window.
